Happy to. First: which level do you want? Story (does it work as a scene), structure (cuts, coverage, continuity), or technical (focus, exposure, sound)? Offline I can measure the technical stuff from the file itself. Story and structure I'd need the speaking model for, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Sure! Tell me the level: story, structure, or technical. Technical I can do right now by measuring the file: sharpness, exposure, audio levels, cut points. For story or structure I need my speaking model connected.

patterns: \b(editing|edit(ing)? (basics|workflow|process|tips)|assembly|rough cut|fine cut|picture lock|how do i edit|first cut)\b
responses: The usual order: organize and review everything, build an assembly of the best takes in script order, tighten to a rough cut, refine the pacing and performances in a fine cut, then lock the picture before sound mix and color. Story first, polish later. Don't color or mix a scene you might still cut.

Editing is rewriting with picture. Watch all the footage once, mark the good takes, assemble the scene, then trim. Cut what doesn't move the story, even if it's pretty. Leave it a day and watch it fresh.

A few classics: cut on action so the movement hides the cut. An L-cut keeps the previous shot's audio running over the next picture; a J-cut starts the next shot's audio before its picture. Hold on reactions, because that's where the audience feels it. And cut when the information is delivered, not after.
Rhythm comes from the length of shots. Let important moments breathe, speed up the boring ones. Dissolves suggest time passing. Hard cuts are the default, and they're good.

patterns: \b(grading|lut|luts|log footage|waveform|vectorscope|scopes?|white balance in post|look of the film)\b
responses: Correct first, then grade. Fix exposure, contrast, and white balance so shots match. Use the waveform for brightness and the vectorscope for color; your eyes lie after a long session. Then apply the look. If you shot in a log format, you'll need a LUT or a color-managed workflow to see normal contrast. DaVinci Resolve's free version is a serious grading tool.
Match shots within a scene before you stylize anything. Skin tones live along a line on the vectorscope, a handy check. Keep the look consistent across the film, and check it on more than one screen.

A mix is built in layers: dialogue first, then effects and foley, then music. Dialogue is king, so everything else sits around it. Typical steps: clean the dialogue, high-pass around 80 Hz to remove rumble, light compression for consistency, a de-esser if the S sounds are harsh, then duck the music under speech. Foley and ADR replace or add the sounds recorded poorly on set.

Mix to the destination. Broadcast usually asks for about -23 LUFS (EBU) or -24 LKFS (US); web platforms commonly sit around -14 to -16. Check the exact spec where you're delivering, because they change. Leave headroom, never let the true peak clip, and listen on cheap speakers and headphones too.

Room tone fills the gaps between lines so the cuts don't pop. If you don't have it, I can build some from the quiet bits. Foley is footsteps, cloth, and props recorded to picture; ADR is re-recording dialogue in a booth. Both are about matching the room and the performance.

Housekeeping saves projects. Name files consistently, keep raw footage read-only, and follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two kinds of media, one off-site. If playback chokes, make proxies (small copies) to edit with and relink to the originals when you export.
Before you edit: copy the footage, verify the copies, back up, and organize into folders for footage, audio, graphics, and exports. Version your project files. Future you will be grateful.

Keep a high-quality master, then make delivery versions. H.264 is the safe default for sharing. Match the frame rate of the source. Check the platform's current specs for resolution, aspect ratio, bitrate, and loudness before you export, because they change over time.
Export the master first and keep it. Then compress for each platform. Watch the whole export on a different device before you send it, because most problems show up there.

Mild shake can be smoothed in post with a warp stabilizer. Resolve and Blender both have a stabilizer, but they crop in a bit and can add a wobbly look. It can't fix motion blur. For the next shoot, ask Pete for a tripod, a gimbal, or a faster shutter.
Stabilizing means analyzing the motion and counter-moving the frame, so you lose some edge. If the shake is heavy, you may need to scale up and lose resolution. Prevention beats the cure here.

Subtitles and captions are text tracks. Most editors can import or create them, and platforms accept an SRT file. Keep lines short, around 32 to 42 characters per line, two lines at most, and on screen long enough to read. Captions also include sound descriptions.

Free and capable: DaVinci Resolve (editing, color, sound, effects in one), Shotcut and Kdenlive for simpler editing, and Blender if you want 3D and tracking. Pick one and learn it deeply instead of hopping between several. I'd start with Resolve.

A film look is mostly a stack of small things: good lighting and exposure, controlled contrast with a gentle highlight roll-off, restrained color, a bit of grain, 24 fps with a natural shutter, and shallow depth of field. A LUT can help, but it can't fix flat lighting. Start with the shot, then the grade.

Three routes: if it was shot on a green screen, pull a key. If it wasn't, roto the subject by hand or with an AI-assisted tool such as the Magic Mask in Resolve. Either way you need to clean the edge and match the new background's light and color. Hair is always the hard part.

Ask Sir Purfluous. He's the writer and performer. I handle what happens to the footage afterwards.

A jump cut is two shots of the same subject that are too alike, so the subject seems to hop. The usual fix is the 30-degree rule: change the angle by at least about 30 degrees, or change the shot size, or cover it with a cutaway. Sometimes it's a style choice, which is fine, but it should look chosen.

Jump cuts happen when you cut within the same framing and the subject pops. Fix it with a different angle or size, a cutaway, or a transition that hides it. Interviews often use B-roll for exactly this.

Audio can often be rescued. Free route: open it in Audacity (it's free and open source). Select a second of pure room noise, use Noise Reduction to learn the noise profile, then apply it to the whole track. Don't overdo it or the voice goes watery. Then Normalize or use a Limiter so the levels are consistent.

For rough audio: first fix the recording if you can, because post only helps so much. For cleanup, Audacity's Noise Reduction handles hiss, a high-pass filter around 80 Hz removes rumble, and Loudness Normalization sets the level. For hum, a notch filter at 50 or 60 Hz, depending on your power grid.

Reskinning means keeping the performance and swapping the look. The performance has to be clean first: stable tracking, consistent lighting, and enough resolution to hold the new surface. Fidelity is mostly the quality of the source, the quality of the model and textures (UVs, PBR materials), and how well the new skin gets lit to match the shot. What PubCast itself can do with this I'll walk through properly once I've checked it against the code, because I won't guess.

Fidelity depends on three things: how good the captured performance is, how good the new asset is, and how well they match in light and color. At a pro studio that's tracking, rotoscoping, a lit 3D asset, then compositing with matched grain and lens effects. For PubCast specifics I want to confirm against the build before I tell you something that isn't true.

A pro VFX pipeline, roughly: previs and planning, then the shoot with clean plates and reference (lens grids, HDRIs, color charts, tracking markers), then tracking or matchmove, then roto and paint, then modeling, texturing, rigging, animation, lighting and rendering for CG, then compositing everything, then review and fixes, then delivery. Most trouble comes from skipping the on-set reference.

At professional studios everything is organized by shots: a plate comes in, gets tracked, the CG is built and lit to match, a compositor marries them, and a supervisor reviews daily. The big lesson is to capture reference on set. A cheap clean plate saves days of paint work.

From the post side, a key is only as good as the plate. Pull the key, clean the matte, then despill and match the edges and the light to the new background. Hair and motion blur are the hard parts. How it should be lit and shot is Pete's side, so ask her to light the screen evenly and keep the subject away from it.

In post: key, matte cleanup, despill, edge treatment, then match color, contrast, and grain to the background. Heavy compression ruins keys, so ask for the least compressed footage the camera can record.

Matchmoving recovers the real camera's movement so a 3D object sits in the shot. It needs parallax (the camera must actually move, not just pan), good texture in the scene, tracking markers when the background is plain, and the lens details. Free options exist: Blender has a motion tracker built in.

For a track: shoot with the camera moving through space, add markers on blank walls, write down the lens and sensor size, and avoid heavy motion blur. If the camera only rotates on a tripod you can't recover depth.

Roto is hand-cutting a subject out of a shot, frame by frame or with keyframed shapes and a bit of interpolation. It's slow but reliable when keying isn't an option. Use fewer, smarter points, keep edges soft where there's motion blur, and track the shapes to the footage where you can.
Rotoscoping is the fallback when you couldn't shoot a clean key. Work in layers (head, torso, arms) so each moves independently, and expect to spend more time on the edges than on the middle.

Compositing makes separate pieces look like they were shot together: match black and white levels, color temperature, grain, lens softness, and add light wrap and shadows. The most common giveaway is mismatched contrast. If it looks pasted on, check the blacks first.
The checklist: edges, color, contrast, grain, shadows, and motion blur. If the foreground and the background don't share the same black level and noise, the eye catches it fast.

Motion capture records a performer's movement and maps it to a rig. Pro studios use camera systems with markers or inertial suits. Cheaper routes exist, such as markerless video capture. The main work is cleanup: foot sliding, jitter, and retargeting to a character with different proportions. I'll go through what PubCast supports once I've checked its modules.

Free stuff I'd trust: Blender (3D, tracking, compositing, editing; blender.org), DaVinci Resolve free edition (editing, color, and the Fusion compositor; from Blackmagic Design), Audacity (audio cleanup), Krita (painting and textures), OBS Studio (recording), and ffmpeg (converting and inspecting media). For textures and lighting reference, Poly Haven offers free HDRIs and materials. Tell me what you're making and I'll help you pick.

Starting kit with no cost: Blender for 3D and tracking, Resolve free for editing and color, Audacity for sound, Krita for textures, OBS for capture, ffmpeg for conversions. Pair them with free texture and HDRI libraries like Poly Haven. Tell me what you're trying to make and I'll narrow it down.

Quick format guide: resolution is detail, frame rate is motion (24 for film feel, 30 or 60 for video), bitrate and codec decide how much quality survives. For effects work, shoot in the least-compressed form you can store and export to a delivery codec like H.264 at the end. Heavy compression makes keying and tracking much harder.
Keep your source high quality and your delivery small. H.264 is great for sharing and poor for effects work. Intermediate codecs such as ProRes or DNxHR survive repeated editing better.
